projects.title: Far Side ISS Commemorative Coin
projects.sub: Cast silver coins for a Space Force research mission
projects.place: U.S. Air Force Academy / International Space Station
projects.lead: A small edition of hand cast .999 silver coins carrying a Gary Larson Far Side image to the International Space Station.
credits: Mission coordination: Maj. Travis Tubbs, U.S. Air Force Academy
Far Side artwork courtesy FarWorks, Inc.
projects.materials: .999 silver, lost wax cast from 3D printed resin

story.label: The work
text: A mission team at the U.S. Air Force Academy wanted to honor Gary Larson and the curiosity The Far Side has inspired in a generation of scientists, by flying one of his images to the International Space Station and returning it to him. The image chosen was his Earth as a balloon, “Listen, I think we better keep this quiet,” first published October 4, 1980. The other face carries the mission's Ad Astra imagery.

story.label: The material question
text: It could not be a minted challenge coin. A tribute to one artist had to be an object made by hand, in a tiny edition, with no permanent die, every file and mold accountable to the rights holders. And it had to fit a spaceflight payload: small, light, and cleared for flight.

story.label: The making
text: We translated Larson's 2D drawing into 3D relief, a conversion the mission lead called amazing work, then printed each coin in castable jewelry resin, burned it out, and poured it in .999 silver, about 1.5 inches across and an eighth of an inch thick. The final geometry needed a much larger cup and sprue than early tests, so each coin took far more silver to pour than it weighs. Files and production materials could be relinquished or destroyed at the end of the run, as the permissions required.

story.label: In place
text: After nearly two years of permissions, proofs and payload changes, the coins launched on May 15 [2026], bound for the International Space Station aboard the Polaris 2026 mission. [Docking / return to Gary Larson: confirm status.]

projects.title: Litowitz Family Office
projects.lead: Dark patinated, bronze finished steel and reeded glass partitions, shelving and doors across a family office floor, built and installed with union crews.
credits: Client: LFO Management / Litowitz Family Office
Union steel and install: Caputo Steel Erectors
projects.materials: Steel patinated dark and bronze finished, reeded glass

story.label: The work
text: A sixth floor build out for the Litowitz Family Office at 1616 Orrington in Evanston: demountable steel and glass partitions, boardroom and elevator entry assemblies, library and lounge metalwork, and back bar and column shelving, all in one dark bronze steel and glass language from the elevator lobby through the boardrooms to the lounge.

story.label: The material question
text: A whole floor had to read as one room. The steel grid had to land on the millwork, the soffits, and the building's pipes without a single misaligned line, and reeded glass had to soften the office for privacy without closing it off from the light and the view of the city.

story.label: The making
text: We drew and redrew the grid against the millwork shop drawings, removed a vertical mullion where a pipe could not move, and extended a soffit so the geometry stayed symmetrical from the lobby through the lounge. Back bar and column shelving went in with Houdini GL-02 reeded glass. Details ran down to perforated metal panels in the boardrooms, blackened and bronze thresholds with a floor grip treatment, elevator entry ceiling panels, custom doors and hardware. The steel was patinated dark, then given a bronze finish. We fabricated the system and directed union installers on site.

projects.title: Palimpsest
projects.sub: Industry of the Ordinary, Driehaus Museum
projects.lead: A Driehaus Museum doorknob, 3D scanned and recast in clay taken from the Chicago River.
credits: Exhibition: Materialities, curated by Giovanni Aloi

story.label: The work
text: After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, new buildings had to be brick or stone, and builders dug clay from the bed of the Chicago River to make the bricks that rebuilt the Nickerson Mansion, now the Driehaus Museum. Industry of the Ordinary took a brass doorknob from one of the doors that separates the family rooms from the servants' quarters and remade it in Chicago River clay, laid on a prone facsimile of its door: a trapdoor between upstairs and downstairs, and a work about the labor that grand houses make invisible.

story.label: The material question
text: An exact copy of a museum object, in a material that fights precision. The original could not leave its door, and river clay shrinks and moves as it dries and fires, so the duplicate had to come from data, then survive the kiln still reading as that particular knob.

story.label: The making
text: We 3D scanned the knob and its plate in place at the museum, cleaned the scan into a model, and split it into molds for the knob and the backplate. Test pieces were pressed and fired [at more than one temperature] to dial in shrinkage and color. [Confirm the process: scanning, modeling, molds, pressing and firing. Who dug and prepared the clay?]

story.label: In place
text: Shown in Materialities at the Driehaus Museum from February 7 to April 27, 2025. The artists thanked Matthew Groves, H Schenck, Ally Reza and Ben Stagl. It was our second project with Industry of the Ordinary, after the cast glass Apple.
